# AWS Serverless Lambda

## Introduction

- A new paradigm, dev don’t have to manage servers, just deploy code  
- Serverless \= FaaS (Function as a Service)  
- Pioneered by AWS Lambda but not also includes anything that’s managed: databases, messaging, storage  
- Serverless means don’t manage / provision / see server

### Serverless in AWS

- AWS Lambda	  
- DynamoDB  
- AWS Cognito  
- AWS API Gateway  
- S3  
- SNS & SQS  
- Kinesis Data Firehose  
- Aurora Serverless  
- Step Functions  
- Fargate

## Overview

### Why Lambda

#### EC2

- Virtual Servers in the Cloud  
- Limited by RAM and CPU  
- Continuously running  
- Scaling means intervention to add/remove servers

#### Lambda

- Virtual functions \- no servers to mange  
- Limited by time \- short executions  
- Run on-demand  
- Scaling is automated

### Benefits

- Easy pricing  
  - Pay per request and compute time  
  - Free tier of 1m requests and 400k GBs of compute time  
- Integrated with many AWS services  
- Integrated with many programming languages  
- Easy to monitoring through AWS cloudwatch  
- Easy to get more resources per functions (up to 10GB of RAM)  
- Increasing RAM will also improve CPI and network

### Lambda language support

- Node.js (JavaScript)  
- Python  
- Java  
- C\# (.NET Core) / Powershell  
- Ruby  
- Custom Runtime API (community supported, Rust or Golang)  
- Lambda Container Image  
  - Container image must implement Lambda Runtime API  
  - ECS / Fargate is preferred for running arbitrary Docker images

### Lambda Pricing

- Pay per calls:  
  - First 1m requests are free  
  - $0.2 per 1m requests thereafter ($0.0000002 per request)  
- Pay per duration (in increments of 1ms)  
  - 400k GB-seconds of compute time per month is free  
  - \== 400k seconds if function is 1GB RAM  
  - \== 3.2m seconds if function is 128 MB RAM  
  - After that $1.00 for 600k GB-seconds  
- Very cheap to run AWS Lambda \-\> very popular

##  Synchronous Invocations

- Synchronous: CLI, SDK, API Gateway, Application load balancer  
  - Results is returned right away  
  - Error handling must happen client side (retries, exponential backoff,..)

### Services

- User invoked:  
  - Elastic Load Balancing (Application load balancer)  
  - Aws api gateway  
  - aws cloudfront (Lambda@Edge)  
  - S3 Batch  
- Service invoked  
  - AWS Cognito  
  - AWS Step Functions  
- Other services  
  - AWS Lex  
  - AWS Alexa  
  - AWS Kinesis Data Firehose

##  Lambda Integration with Application Load Balancer

- To expose a Lambda function as an HTTP(S) endpoint

##  Asynchronous Invocations & DLQ

- S3, SNS, Cloudwatch events…  
- Events placed in an Event Queue  
- Lambda retry on errors(3 tries total: 1min wait after 1st, then 2min wait)  
- Make sure the processing is idempotent(result is the same after retries)  
- If retried, then duplicate logs entries in Cloudwatch Logs  
- Define DLQ \- SNS or SQS for failed processing (need correct IAM permissions)  
- Asynchronous invocations allow speed up processing

### Services

- S3  
- SNS  
- EventBridge  
- CodeCommit (trigger: new branch, tag, push)  
- CodePipeline (during pipeline, Lambda must callback)  
- Cloudwatch Logs  
- Simple Email Service  
- AWS CloudFormation  
- AWS Config  
- AWS IoT  
- AWS IoT Events

2 way to trigger:

##  S3 Event Notifications

- S3:ObjectCreated, S3:ObjectRemoved, S3:ObjectRestore, S3:Replication,..  
- Object name filtering possible (\*.jpg)  
- Use case: generate thumbnails of images upload to S3  
- S3 event notifications typically deliver events in seconds but sometimes take a minutes ỏ longer  
- If two writes are made to a single non-versioned object at the same time, it is possible that only a single event will be sent  
- Enable versioning on bucket to ensure event is sent for every successful write

### Simple S3 Event Pattern \- Metadata Sync

S3 bucket \-\> Lambda	\-\> RDS or DynamoDB Table

##  Lambda \- Event Source Mapping

- Kinesis data streams  
- SQS & SQS FIFO queue  
- Dynamodb Streams  
- Common denominator: records need to be polled from source  
- Invoke synchronously

### Streams & Lambda (Kinesis & DynamoDB)

- Iterator for each shard, processes items in order  
- Start with new items, from the beginning or from timestamp  
- Processed items not remoted from stream(other can read)  
- Low traffic: use batch window to accumulate records before processing  
- Process multiple batches in parallel(one shard)  
  - Up to 10 batches per shard  
  - In-order processing is still guaranteed for each partition key

### Streams & Lambda \- Error Handling

- Default, if error then entire batch reprocessed until succeeds, or items in batch expire  
- Because in-order so affected shard paused until error is resolved  
- Config event source to:  
  - Discard old events  
  - Restrict number of retries  
  - Split batch on error(to work around Lambda timeout issues)  
- Discarded events can go to a Destination

### SQS & SQS FIFO

- Event Source Mapping will poll SQS (Long Polling)  
- Specify batch size (1-10 messages)  
- Recommend: set queue visibility to 6x Lambda function timeout  
- Use DLQ  
  - Setup on SQS queue, not Lambda(DLQ for Lambda is only for async invocations)  
  - Or use Lambda destination for failures

### Queue & Lambda

- Lambda also supports in-order processing for FIFO queues, scaling up to the number of active message groups  
- For standard queues, items aren’t processed in order and Lambda scales up to process as quickly as possible  
- When error occurs, batches are returned to queue as individual items and might be processed in different grouping than the original batch  
- Occasionally, event source mapping might receive same item twice from queue, even if no function error occurred  
- Lambda deletes items from queue after processed successfully  
- Can configure source queue to send items to DLQ if they can’t processed

### Lambda Event Mapper Scaling

- Kinesis Data Streams & DynamoDB Streams  
  - One Lambda invocation per stream shard  
  - Parallel up to 10 batches per shard simultaneously  
- SQS standard  
  - Lambda adds 60 more instances per minute to scale up  
  - Up to 1000 batches of messages processed simultaneously  
- SQS FIFO  
  - Messages with same GroupID will be processed in order  
  - Lambda function scales to number of active message groups

##  Event  & Context Object

- Event object  
  - JSON-formatted contains data for the function to process  
  - Information from invoking service (EventBridge, custom, …)  
  - Lambda runtime converts event to an object (e.g.,dict type in Python)  
  - Example: input argos, invoking service args,...  
- Context object  
  - Provides methods and properties about the invocation, function, runtime environment  
  - Pass to function by Lambda at runtime  
  - Example: aws\_request\_id, function\_name, memory\_limit\_in\_mb,..

##  Destinations

- From November 2019, can configure to send result to a destination  
- Asynchronous invocations: both successful and failed event:  
  - SQS  
  - SNS  
  - Lambda  
  - EventBridge  
- Note: AWS recommends use destinations instead of DLQ now  
- Event Source mapping: for discarded event batches  
  - SQS  
  - SNS  
- Note: can send events to a DLQ directly from SQS  
- When setup failure destination, lambda invoke and retries for 2 times before send to destination

##  Permissions \- IAM Roles & Resource Policies

### Lambda execution role (IAM Role)

- Grants Lambda function permissions to AWS services/resources  
- Sample managed policies for Lambda:  
  - AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole \- Upload logs to Cloudwatch  
  - AWSLambdaKinesisExecutionRole \- Read from Kinesis  
- When use Event Source Mapping to invoke function, Lambda uses the execution role to read event data  
- Best practice: create one Lambda Execution Role per function

### Lambda Resource Based Policies

- Use resource-based policies to give other accounts and AWS services permission to use Lambda resources  
- Similar to S3 bucket policies  
- An IAM principal can access Lambda  
  - If IAM policy attached to the principal authorizes it (e.g. User access)  
  - OR if the resource-based policy authorizes (e.g. service access)  
- When AWS service like S3 calls Lambda function, the resource-based policy gives it access

##  Lambda Environment Variables

- Environment variable \= key / value pair  
- Lambda service adds its own system variables as well  
- Helpful to store secrets (encrypted by KMS)  
- Secrets can be encrypted by Lambda service key, or CMK (customer master key)

## Lambda Monitoring & X-Ray Tracing

### Logging & Monitoring

- Cloudwatch logs:  
  - Stored in AWS Cloudwatch logs  
  - Make sure Lambda function has an execution role with an IAM policy (writes to Cloudwatch logs)  
- Cloudwatch metrics:  
  - AWS Lambda metrics are displayed in AWS Cloudwatch Metrics  
  - Invocations, Durations, Concurrent Executions  
  - Error count, Success Rates, Throttles  
  - Async Delivery Failures  
  - Iterator Age (Kinesis & DynamoDB Streams)

### Tracing

- Enable in Lambda configuration (Active Tracing)  
- Runs the X-Ray daemon for you  
- Use AWS X-Ray SDK in Code  
- Ensure Lambda Function has correct IAM Execution Role  
  - Managed policy is AWSXRayDaemonWriteAccess  
- Environment variables to communicate with X-Ray  
  - \_X\_AMZN\_TRACE\_ID contains tracing header  
  - AWS\_XRAY\_CONTEXT\_MISSING  
    - RUNTIME\_ERROR – Throw a runtime exception.  
    - LOG\_ERROR – Log an error and continue (default).  
    - IGNORE\_ERROR – Ignore error and continue.  
  - AWS\_XRAY\_DAEMON\_ADDRESS: X-Ray Daemon IP\_ADDRESS:PORT

## Lambda@Edge & CloudFront Functions

### Customization at the Edge

- Modern apps execute logic at the edge  
- Edge functions:  
  - Code attached to Aws cloudfront distributions  
  - Runs close to users to minimize latency  
- CloudFront provides 2 types: CloudFront Functions & Lambda@Edge  
- Don’t have to manage any servers, deployed globally  
- Use case: customize CDN content  
- Pay only for using  
- Fully serverless

### Use cases

- Web Security and Privacy  
- Dynamic web app at the Edge  
- Search engine optimization (SEO)  
- Intelligently Route Across Origins and Data Centers  
- Bot Mitigation at the Edge  
- Real-time Image Transformation  
- A/B Testing  
- User Authentication and Authorization  
- User Prioritization  
- User tracking and analytics

### CloudFront Functions

- Lightweight functions written in JavaScript  
- For high-scale, latency-sensitive CDN customizations  
- Sub-ms startup times, millions of requests per second  
- Used to change Viewer requests and responses:  
  - Viewer Request: after Cloudfront receives a request  
  - Viewer Response: before Cloudfront forwards response  
- Native feature of Cloudfront

### Lambda@Edge

- Lambda functions written in NodeJS or Python  
- Scales to 1000s of requests/second  
- Used to change Cloudfront requests and responses:  
  - Viewer request \- after Cloudfront receives a request from viewer  
  - Origin request \- before Cloudfront forwards requests to origin  
  - Origin response \- after Cloudfront receives response from origin  
  - Viewer response \- before cloudfront forwards response to the viewer  
- Author functions in one AWS Region, then Cloudfront replicates to all of its locations

Use cases:

| Cloudfront Functions | Lambda@Edge |
| :---- | :---- |
| Cache key normalization, transform  request attributes (headers, cookies, query strings, URL) to create optimal Cache Key Header manipulation URL rewrites or redirects Request auth: create, validate user-generated tokens | Longer execution time (several ms) Adjustable CPU or memory Code depends on 3rd libraries (e.g, AWS SDK to access other AWS services) Network access to use external services for processing File system access or access to HTTP request body |

## Lambda in VPC

### By default

- Lambda function is launched outside VPC (AWS-owned VPC)  
- Can not access resources in VPC (RDS, ElastiCache, internal ELB,...)

### In VPC

- Must define VPC ID, Subnets and Security Groups  
- Lambda will create an ENI (Elastic Network Interface) in subnets  
- Need AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole

### Internet access

- Default, Lambda function in VPC not have internet access  
- Deploying Lambda function in public subnet does not give it internet access or public IP  
- Deploying Lambda function in private subnets gives it internet access if have NAT Gateway / Instance  
- Use VPC endpoints to privately access AWS services without a NAT

## Lambda Function Performance

### Configuration

- RAM  
  - From 128MB to 10GB, in 1MB increments  
  - More RAM add, more vCPU credits get  
  - At 1792 MB, a function has the equivalent of one full vCPU  
  - After 1792MB, get more than 1 CPU, need to use multi-threading in code to benefit from it  
- If app is CPU-bound(heavy compute), increase RAM  
- Timeout: default 3s, max 900s(15m)

### Lambda Execution Context

- Temporary runtime environment that initializes any external dependencies  
- Great for database connections, HTTP clients, SDK clients,..  
- Maintained for some time in anticipation of another Lambda function invocation  
- Next function invocation can “re-use” context to save time in initializing connections objects  
- The execution context includes /tmp directory

### Lambda Functions /tmp space

- Needs to download big file to work  
- Needs disk space to perform operations  
- Max 10GB  
- Directory content remains when execution context is frozen, providing transient cache for multiple invocations(helpful to checkpoint work)  
- For permanent persistence \-\> S3  
- To encrypt content on /tmp \-\> must generate KMS Data Keys

## Lambda Layers

- Custom runtimes  
- Externalize Dependencies to re-use

## Lambda File Systems Mounting

- Lambda functions can access EFS file systems if in a VPC  
- Configure Lambda to mount EFS file systems to local directory during initialization  
- Must leverage EFS access points  
- Limitations: EFS connection limits (1 function \= 1 connection) and connection burst limits

## Lambda Concurrency and Throttling

- Limit: up to 1000 concurrent executions  
- Set “reserved concurrency” at function level  
- Throttle behavior  
  - Synchronous invocation \=\> ThrottleError \- 429  
  - Asynchronous invocation \=\> Auto retry and then to DLQ  
- If need higher limit then open a support ticket

### Concurrency and Asynchronous Invocations

- If function doesn’t have enough concurrency available to process events, additional request are throttled  
- For throttling errors (429) and system errors(500), Lambda returns event to queue and attempts again for up to 6 hours  
- Retry interval increases exponentially from 1s after first attempt to max 5 mins

### Cold start & Provisioned Concurrency

- Cold start  
  - New instance \=\> code is loaded and code outside the handler run (init)  
  - If the init is large (code, dependencies, SDK..) this process can take time  
  - First request served by new instances has higher latency than the rest  
- Provisioned concurrency  
  - Concurrency is allocated before function is invoked  
  - Cold start never happens and all invocations have low latency  
  - Application Auto Scaling can manage concurrency (schedule or target utilization)  
- Note: cold starts in VPC reduced in Oct & Nov 2019

## Lambda External Dependencies

- If Lambda depends on external libs \-\> need install packages and zip it  
  - Node.js, use npm &  “node\_modules” directory  
  - Python, use pip –target options  
  - Java, include relevant .jar files  
- Upload zip to Lambda if less than 50MB, else to S3 first  
- Native libraries work: need to complied on Amazon Linux  
- AWS SDK comes by default with every Lambda function

## Lambda and CloudFormation

### Inline

- Inline functions are very simple  
- Use Code.ZipFile property  
- Can not include functions dependencies with inline functions

### S3

- Store Lambda in S3  
- Must refer S3 zip location in CloudFormation code:  
  - S3Bucket  
  - S3Key: full path to zip  
  - S3ObjectVersion: if versioned bucket  
- If update code in S3, don’t update S3Bucket, S3Key or S3ObjectVersion, CloudFormation won’t update function

## Lambda Container Images

- Deploy Lambda function as container images of up to 10GB from ECR  
- Pack complex dependencies, large dependencies in a container  
- Base images are available for Python, [Node.js](http://Node.js), Java, .NET, Go, Ruby  
- Can create own image as long as it implements Lambda Runtime API  
- Test containers locally using Lambda Runtime Interface Emulator  
- Unified workflow to build apps

### Best Practices

Strategies for optimizing container images:

- Use AWS-provided Base Images  
  - Stable, build on Amazon Linux 2, cache by Lambda service  
- Use multi-stage builds  
  - Build code in larger preliminary images, copy only artifacts needed in final container, discard preliminary steps  
- Build from stable to frequently changing  
  - Most frequently occurring changes as late in Dockerfile as possible  
- Use single repository for Functions with Large Layers  
  - ECR compares each layer of image when it pushed to avoid uploading and storing duplicates  
- Use when upload large Lambda Functions (Up to 10GB)

## Lambda Versions and Aliases

### Versions

- Work on $LATEST  
- When publish Lambda, we create a version  
- Versions are immutable  
- Versions have increasing version numbers  
- Versions get their own ARN(Amazon Resource Name)  
- Version \= code \+ configuration (nothing can be changed \- immutable)  
- Each version can be accessed

### Alias

- Point to Lambda function versions  
- Define dev, test, prod aliases and point at different lambda versions  
- Aliases are mutable  
- Aliases enable Canary deployment by assigning weights to lambda functions  
- Aliases enable stable configuration of event triggers / destinations  
- Aliases have their own ARN  
- Aliases cannot reference aliases

## Lambda and CodeDeploy

- CodeDeploy help automate traffic shift for Lambda alias  
- Feature is integrated within SAM framework  
- Linear: grow traffic every N minutes until 100%  
  - Linear10PercentEvery3Minutes  
  - Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes  
- Canary: try X percent then 100%  
  - Canary10Percent5Minutes  
  - Canary10Percent30Minutes  
- AllAtOnce: immediate  
- Can create Pre & Post Traffic hooks to check health of Lambda function

### AppSpec.yml

- Name (required) \- name of Lambda function to deploy  
- Alias (required) \- name of alias to Lambda function  
- CurrentVersion (required) \- version of Lambda function traffic currently points to  
- TargetVersion (required) \- version of Lambda function traffic is shifted to

## Lambda function URL

### Function URL

- Dedicated HTTP(S) endpoint for Lambda function  
- Unique URL endpoint generated (never changes)  
  - https://\<url-id\>.lambda-url.\<region\>.on.aws (dual-stack IPv4 & IPv6)  
- Invoke via web browser, curl, postman, ..  
- Access function URL through public Internet only  
  - Doesn’t support PrivateLink  
- Support Resource-based Policies & CORS configurations  
- Applied to any function alias or to $LATEST (can’t applied to other function versions)  
- Create and configure using AWS Console or AWS API  
- Throttle function by using Reserved Concurrency

### Function URL Security

- Resource-based Policy  
  - Authorize other accounts / specific CIDR / IAM principals  
- Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)  
  - Call Lambda function from different domain  
- AuthType NONE \- allow public and unauthenticated access	  
  - Resource-based Policy is always in effect (must grant public access)  
- AuthType AWS\_IAM \- IAM used to authenticate and authorize requests  
  - Both Principal’s Identity-based Policy & Resource-based Policy are evaluated  
  - Principal must have lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl permissions  
  - Same account \- Identity-based Policy OR Resource-based Policy as ALLOW  
  - Cross account \- Identity-based Policy AND Resource-based Policy as ALLOW

## Lambda CodeGuru Integration

- Gain insights into runtime performance of Lambda functions using CodeGuru Profiler  
- CodeGuru creates a Profiler Group for Lambda function  
- Supported for Java and Python runtimes  
- Activate from AWS Lambda Console  
- When activated, Lambda adds:  
  - CodeGuru Profiler layer to function  
  - Environment variables to function  
  - AmazonCodeGuruProfilerAgentAccess policy to function

## Lambda Limits

- Execution  
  - Mem allocation: 128MB-10GB (1MB unit)  
  - Max execution time 900s (15m)  
  - Environment variables(4KB)  
  - Disk capacity in function container (/tmp) 512MB to 10GB  
  - Concurrency executions: 1000 (can be increased)  
- Deployment  
  - Lambda function deployment size (compressed .zip) 50MB  
  - Size of uncompressed deployment (code \+ dependencies): 250MB  
  - Can use /tmp directory to load other files at startup  
  - Size of environment variable: 4KB

## AWS Lambda Best Practices

- Perform heavy-duty work outside of function handler  
  - Connect db outside function handler  
  - Initialize AWS SDK outside function handler  
  - Pull in dependencies or datasets outside function handler  
- Use environment variables for:  
  - Db connection strings, S3 bucket, … don’t put in code  
  - Passwords, sensitive values can be encrypted using KMS  
- Minimize deployment package size to runtime  
  - Break down function if needed  
  - Remember limits  
  - Use Layers where necessary  
- Avoid using recursive code, never have Lambda function call itself
